label: Storms and quakes
rationale: The big events people warn each other about, and the forecast that got it wrong: a typhoon on the way, an earthquake, thunder, a missed forecast.
mixUps: English 'hit' fits none of them: a typhoon kuru (comes), an earthquake okiru (happens; jishin kita as it shakes) and thunder naru (sounds), so drill the three verbs side by side. kaminari ga naru is 鳴る 'sound', not naru 'become', and a forecast hazureru (misses) or ataru (is right), never machigaeru.

targets.trap: English 'a typhoon hits' pushes to taifuu ga utsu or taifuu ga ataru, which don't work: with the typhoon as subject it just comes (taifuu kita). Ataru is fine the other way round, with your plans as subject and ni: ryokou ga taifuu ni atatchatta (our trip ran into a typhoon). Chokugeki (direct hit) is everyday talk too: toukyou chokugeki rashii yo (apparently it's heading straight for Tokyo); jouriku (landfall) mostly comes from the forecast.
partners: jishin (earthquake: jishin kita! as it shakes; the usual set is jishin ga okiru)
targets.use: Mostly said without ga, about one in the forecast: shuumatsu taifuu kuru kamo (a typhoon might come this weekend). Taifuu kiteru means one has already come close and is nearby or heading in, not a forecast for later in the week; taifuu chikazuiteru stresses that it's getting closer, and taifuu kita means it has arrived. Often there's no verb at all: ashita taifuu da tte (they say there's a typhoon tomorrow).
targets.notes: The cause takes de: taifuu de densha tomatta (the trains stopped because of the typhoon); once it's passed, taifuu sugita ne.

example.ja: 明日台風来るらしいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: ashita taifuu ga kuru rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 明日台風が来るらしいですよ。

targets.verbSense: happen, occur; also wake up, get up
targets.trap: English 'an earthquake hit' has no matching verb, and utsu or ataru don't work. It happens (okiru), or casually it comes or there is one (jishin kita!, jishin atta).
targets.use: Used when talking about a quake: jishin ga okita toki (when the earthquake hit), ookii jishin ga okitara (if a big one hits). In the moment people shout jishin da! or jishin kita!, and afterwards say kinou jishin atta ne.
targets.notes: The shaking is yureru: ima yureta? (did it just shake?), kekkou yureta ne.

example.ja: 大きい地震起きたらどうする？
example.english: What would you do if a big earthquake hit?

examplePolite.romaji: ookii jishin ga okitara dou shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大きい地震が起きたらどうしますか？
examplePolite.english: What would you do if a big earthquake hit?

targets.verbSense: make a sound, ring (thunder, a phone, a bell, an alarm)
targets.use: Said when you hear thunder: kaminari natteru (it's thundering), or kaminari natta! for a single clap. Casual speech drops ga.
targets.notes: Naru here is 鳴る 'ring' (as in denwa ga naru), said flat (na-RU), while naru 'become' falls (NA-ru). A strike is kaminari ga ochiru: chikaku ni ochita! The flash is kaminari ga hikaru.

targets.kana: てんきよほうがはずれる
targets.verbSense: miss, come off; turn out wrong (a forecast, guess, lottery ticket)
targets.trap: A forecast misses (hazureru) or hits (ataru), like a guess or a lottery ticket. Machigaeru is a person's slip, so yohou ga machigaeta doesn't work; yohou machigatteta (it was wrong) is also fine, but hazureta is the usual word.
targets.use: A grumble, almost always in the past: tenki yohou hazureta (the forecast got it wrong), usually without ga, or just yohou hazureta once the weather is already the topic. When it gets it right: yohou atatta.
targets.notes: What it says: yohou de wa ame da tte (the forecast says rain).

example.ja: 天気予報、また外れたね。
example.english: The forecast got it wrong again.

examplePolite.ja: 天気予報、また外れましたね。
examplePolite.english: The forecast got it wrong again.

reviewPool.english: be late for the train (and so miss it)
the last train is gone (no way home)
wake up (from sleep); feel wide awake (me ga sameta)
get into bed, get under the covers
